correctness.rationale: Partition all \(0<p\le t\le1\) into the five threshold strips. For the first strip, any successful outcome requires at least one success. In the next two strips, count winning singleton stakes and bound conditional success by binomial tail counts; subtracting the proposed optimum gives \((3-s)p(1-p)^3\), \(p(1-p)^2(1-2p)\), or \(p(1-p)^2(2-3p)\), all nonnegative in the stipulated ranges. For thresholds above 1/2, winning pairs form an intersecting graph on four vertices, hence a star or triangle; star/triangle bounds give \(\max\{p,3p^2-2p^3\}\). Above 2/3, a winning triangle is impossible and any winning pair forces every successful set to contain one fixed endpoint; without winning pairs, the three-versus-four winning triple possibilities are bounded respectively by \(3p^3(1-p)+p^4\le p\) and \(4p^3-3p^4\le p\) with the latter requiring \(p\le3/4\). One-, two-, three-, or four-equal-stake vectors attain each upper bound, proving the exact maximum including all boundary thresholds. An exact-rational finite-grid verifier agrees but is not used as a proof.

evidence: The motivating paper proves the unrestricted conjecture for high thresholds with p<=1/2 (Corollary 5.2), exactly t=1/2 with p<=1/2 (Corollary 5.4), and low probabilities p<1/(2k+1) for t>1/(k+1) (Theorem 6.1).
The same paper proves in Corollary 5.3 that one-stake bold play is not optimal for 1/2<p<=t<=2/3; it does not provide the four-position maximum in that entire region.
The Fishburn-et-al. intersecting-family theorem, quoted and used in the motivating paper, handles high-threshold p-biased intersecting systems, not all low-threshold four-coordinate winning families.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Some individual parameter regimes of the new formula are pre-covered, and the result does not claim novelty for those alone. However, no checked theorem applies to every 0<p<=t<=1 with at most four unequal stakes, e.g. p=3/10,t=31/100 lies outside the low-probability sufficient region and t=1/3 special case. A theorem for unrestricted stakes covering that example would dominate this result, but the source explicitly leaves an unshaded gap.

originality.rationale: The closest primary full text states Csóka’s conjecture in unrestricted dimension and solves only portions of the (p,t) region; no theorem in its inspected statements determines all unequal four-stake strategies throughout the parameter triangle. Its general high-threshold results subsume some pieces, a limitation disclosed explicitly. The low-threshold unshaded gap remains; source- and formula-specific online scholarly-index searches and prior-claim implication comparisons revealed no theorem dominating the exact four-stake classification. Residual risk is an equivalent small-dimension weighted-threshold classification in older combinatorics or gambling literature.
residual_risks: A small-n weighted Boolean threshold-family theorem or elementary gambling optimization published under unrelated terminology may already imply the four-stake formula.

value.rationale: This is the first nontrivial full finite-dimensional phase diagram of a published open Bernoulli stake-optimization question with four potentially unequal positions. It gives sharp probabilities for every threshold and bias with p<=t, exhibits the three-bet majority transition at p=1/2, and separates all low-threshold and high-threshold support geometries by a small winning-pair graph. The classification covers parameter values in the published unsolved gap for general stake counts, yet modestly restricts to four stakes without asserting the infinite-dimensional conjecture.
